added_claims.speaker: Nick Baltas

added_claims.claim: A single-stock time-series trend portfolio can be decomposed into cross-sectional momentum (e.g. long 60 and short 40 of 100 stocks equals momentum on 40 plus 20 net long beta); the research question is how much of the return comes from market timing versus the cross-sectional premium.
added_claims.conditions: Applies when the trend portfolio is not market neutral.
added_claims.testable: yes - decompose returns into beta timing and cross-sectional spread

corrections.issue: Says trend was the defensive choice after 2018. Nick said trend did poorly in 2018 and 2020, so investors then bought long volatility; after long vol failed in 2022 (trend delivered) they went back to trend, then felt disappointment with recent V-shaped markets.
corrections.fix: Investors switch defensive products reactively: after trend disappointed in 2018 and 2020 they added long volatility, long vol failed in 2022 while trend delivered, then they returned to trend and were disappointed again by the recent V-shapes, an 'act of regret' that is unhealthy for product design.

corrections.issue: Names a 'Man AHL paper', but the transcript never names the author or firm (the caption reads 'a paper from one that was actually quite nice a couple of months ago').
corrections.fix: An unnamed recent paper compared portfolio compositions: a small concentrated portfolio of macro markets gives positive skew and defensiveness in equity drawdowns, while adding alternative markets maximises long-term expected Sharpe through idiosyncratic bets.

completeness_estimate: 0.80 - first reader caught the main themes (QIS industry, crowding, curve carry drawdown, trend 2026, execution, single-stock trend); it missed secondary points (QIS pros, risk-limit exits, curve-carry long-run record, CTA index composition, alt-market definition, execution value, attribution) and misread the 2018/2020 sequence.
